items.figure: The diagrams show a plant cell and an animal cell, with their visible structures labelled.
steps: On the plant-cell diagram, label the outer thick boundary as cell wall and the boundary just inside it as cell membrane.
Label the material inside the membrane as cytoplasm; label the large central space as vacuole and its boundary as tonoplast.
Label the nucleus and, inside it, the nucleolus and chromatin.
Label the green oval bodies as chloroplasts and the bean-shaped bodies with inner folds as mitochondria.
Label any visible networks of membranes as endoplasmic reticulum and the stack of flattened sacs as Golgi complex.
On the animal-cell diagram, label the outer boundary as cell membrane and the interior as cytoplasm.
Label the nucleus, nucleolus and chromatin; also label any visible mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and centrioles.
Do not label structures that are not shown in the diagrams.
items.finalAnswer: Label the visible parts of the plant and animal cells as described.

steps: The fluid mosaic model describes the structure of the cell membrane.
The membrane consists mainly of a double layer (bilayer) of phospholipid molecules, with proteins embedded in or attached to it.
The hydrophilic heads of the phospholipids face the watery environments inside and outside the cell, while their hydrophobic tails face inward, away from water.
The proteins and phospholipid molecules are not fixed in one position; they can move sideways within the bilayer.
This movement makes the membrane fluid, while the different proteins distributed through the bilayer give it a mosaic appearance.
The membrane is selectively permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
items.finalAnswer: The cell membrane is a selectively permeable, fluid phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it that can move sideways, giving it a mosaic appearance.

steps: The nucleus is usually a large, spherical or oval organelle and acts as the control centre of the cell.
It is surrounded by a double membrane called the nuclear membrane or nuclear envelope, which has pores that allow exchange of materials with the cytoplasm.
The nucleoplasm is the fluid material inside the nuclear membrane.
The nucleolus is a dense body in the nucleoplasm; it is involved in the formation of ribosomes.
Chromatin consists of fine thread-like material in the nucleoplasm. It contains DNA and condenses to form chromosomes during cell division.
The chromosomes carry genes, which contain hereditary information.
items.finalAnswer: The nucleus consists of a pore-bearing double nuclear membrane, nucleoplasm, nucleolus and DNA-containing chromatin; it controls cell activities and carries hereditary information.

steps: Lysosomes are small, spherical sacs surrounded by a single membrane.
They contain digestive enzymes that break down foreign material, worn-out cell parts and other substances; the resulting materials can be reused by the cell.
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membrane-bound channels and flattened sacs in the cytoplasm, often connected to the nuclear membrane.
Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface and is involved in the synthesis and transport of proteins.
Smooth ER has no attached ribosomes and is involved in the synthesis of lipids and the transport of materials.
items.finalAnswer: Lysosomes are single-membrane sacs containing digestive enzymes, while the ER is a network of membrane-bound channels that helps make and transport proteins and lipids.

steps: The Golgi complex is formed from vesicles produced by the endoplasmic reticulum.
It consists of stacks of flattened, membrane-bound sacs called cisternae, with small vesicles often present at their edges.
It modifies, sorts and packages materials such as proteins received from the ER.
The packaged materials are transported in vesicles to other parts of the cell or to the cell membrane for secretion.
The Golgi complex also helps in the formation of lysosomes.
items.finalAnswer: The Golgi complex consists of stacks of flattened sacs that modify, sort and package materials for transport or secretion, and help form lysosomes.

steps: A chloroplast is a green, usually disc-shaped organelle found in plant cells.
It is surrounded by a double membrane and contains a fluid called stroma.
Within the stroma are flattened membrane sacs called thylakoids; these are arranged in stacks called grana.
The thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs light energy.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, using light energy to make food from carbon dioxide and water, and releasing oxygen.
items.finalAnswer: A chloroplast has a double membrane, stroma and chlorophyll-containing thylakoids arranged in grana; it carries out photosynthesis.

steps: Plant cells have a cell wall outside the cell membrane; animal cells do not have a cell wall.
Plant cells usually have chloroplasts; animal cells do not have chloroplasts.
Plant cells usually have one large, central vacuole; animal cells usually have small vacuoles or none.
Animal cells usually have centrioles; plant cells generally do not have centrioles.
Plant cells often have a more fixed, regular shape because of the cell wall; animal cells usually have a more flexible, irregular shape.
items.finalAnswer: Plant cells have a cell wall, usually chloroplasts and a large central vacuole; animal cells lack these features and usually have centrioles.

steps: Division of labour is the distribution of different functions among specialized parts of an organism.
In multicellular organisms, cells become specialized to perform particular functions, and groups of similar cells form tissues.
Different tissues work together in organs, and organs work together in organ systems; this cooperation enables the organism to carry out all necessary life processes efficiently.
Red blood cells transport oxygen around the body.
Nerve cells conduct nerve impulses.
Muscle cells contract to produce movement.
Root hair cells absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.
items.finalAnswer: Division of labour is the sharing of different functions among specialized cells, tissues and organs; examples include oxygen transport by red blood cells, impulse conduction by nerve cells, and movement produced by muscle cells.
